newsitem.title: USA: Resignations at Columbia/HCA draw mixed reactions.
newsitem.headline: Resignations at Columbia/HCA draw mixed reactions.

text.p: The resignations under fire of Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp's two top executives may help it settle its problems with the government and, perhaps, realize a rumored merger with Tenet Healthcare Corp.

But analysts also said Friday that the largest U.S. for-profit hospital company will sorely miss former chief executive Richard Scott's business acumen and, as a result, may have to spin the door to the CEO's suite one more time.
"We view the change as a mixed blessing," said Margo Vignola, healthcare industry analyst at Merrill Lynch.

Not only Scott, but his chief operations officer and president David Vandewater resigned Thursday night after a late-night board meeting called to address mounting concerns about the massive federal investigation that engulfed the company two weeks ago.
Scott had been viewed as a roadblock to resolution of the investigation, but the hard-charging company co-founder was also seen as a demanding manager and a business visionary.
"Without him, growth is likely to stall," Vignola said.
Analysts said they do not see Dr. Thomas Frist, who took over as chairman and chief executive, as a long-term solution.

"I would not call Dr. Frist a caretaker," said Stephen Inc healthcare industry analyst Nancy Weaver. But analysts said Frist may not want a lengthy commitment. As co-founder with his father of Hospital Corp of America, which Columbia later acquired, Frist has made his mark and his fortune. He is one of the richest people in America, according to Forbes magazine. His brother, Bill Frist, is a U.S. senator.

Asked on Friday if he would be a permanent or interim CEO, he said: "I've accepted this job and my challenge is to address the issues before it. I am absolutely committed to addressing those if it take three months, three years or longer."
He added that the top issues facing the company are ending the government probe and focusing on shareholder interests.
"Frist won't be in there for long, but he won't disappear," said one analyst who asked not to be named.

The scenario painted by some analysts featured Jeffrey Barbakow, chairman and chief executive of Tenet Healthcare Corp, as possibly the ultimate successor to Scott -- if, that is, a Columbia-Tener merger is actually in the works.

Scott's resignation "definitely makes it easier to do a deal with Tenet because before you were going to have to decide which management team would be in charge. Now that's not an issue," Weaver said.
Still, there remained uncertainty about the rumored merger.
"We feel it is unlikely that THC and COL would merge anytime soon," said Credit Suisse First Boston healthcare analyst Howard Capek.
